messages.author: 900cd0718d2352a1
messages.subject: Inference in Stan about a distribution using data informative of E(X|X>a & X<b)
parts:
As a simple motivating example, consider a normally distributed variable X, and a dataset that contains the count and average value of X within different ranges from a sample of X-values. 

For instance, we might have a dataset of ranges and averages as follows:

      category count   average
1: (73.9,89.6]    58  84.97311
2:  (89.6,105]   235  98.10409
3:   (105,121]    96 111.14513
4:   (121,137]    11 125.60737

We know the underlying variable X comes from a normal distribution (in this case - the data were simulated with mean 100 and sd 10) and we want to estimate the mean and sd of the distribution.

Can anyone help point me towards some way of coding the model block in Stan to use data of this form to infer the parameters of the distribution generating the X-values? 

Although the illustration uses a normal distribution, I am curious as to whether there is a way of doing this that would work more generally than just in the case of a normal distribution. I've come across several related inference problems that I hope to find a way to code in Stan, where the key is to use information that speaks to the expected value of a distribution conditional on the values being in some specific range, and where I want to use this information to infer the underlying parameters of the distribution involved. Mathematically, I would express this by stating that some observed value is equal to some definite integral - but I haven't found a way to express such relationships in the Stan model block. Is it possible, or is there a "trick" that can be used to reformulate the problem and make it easier to code in Stan?


Sincerely,
Ole

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Inference in Stan about a distribution using data informative of E(X|X>a & X<b)
parts:
As with any model it is best to reason about your problem _generatively_.
Right now the problem you propose has gaping holes which is why it is
so confusing.

The first thing you need is a model for the latent value of x.  Let’s follow
your example and say that it’s Gaussian with unknown mean and standard
deviation,

mu ~ some_prior;
sigma ~ some_prior;
x ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Now you have a censoring process where you get only imitated information
about this distribution.  The binning part is straightforward: the relative
weight of each category is given by integrating the latent distribution between
the boundaries,

p_{i} = normal_cdf(right_bundary | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(left_boundary | mu, sigma);

The likelihood is then naturally a multinomial process,

n ~ multinomial(p, sum(N));

Which you can also approximate with individual Poisson distributions if N is 
big enough,

n_{i} ~ poisson(sum(N) * p_{i});

And for the average?  Well, that’s going to be awkward no matter what given
that it’s hard to come up with a measurement model for “averages”.  Given
the latent distribution for x and the boundaries you can conceivably compute
the true mean in each category, although it won’t be analytic for event this
simple example (unless I’m missing some clever trick).  But even then, if
you knew the exact category means, mu_{i}, how would you define a 
measurement model for “average” data, \bar{x}_{i}?  One immediate issue is that
any reasonable measurement model would corrupt the measured value of
x, causing measurements to move into different categories from which they
were generated.  

In any case, all of that awkwardness is a sure sign that the model you’re trying
to build is not actually representative of a reasonable data generating process.
It may be an awkward approximation of one, but to really understand the
validity of that approximation you’ll want to figure out the proper data generating
process first and then approximate as necessary.
